Source model: `withheld`
Condition: LONG

# The Door on the Number Nine

On the last Thursday of the municipal lost-property office, a woman came in and asked if we had a door.

“What sort of door?” I said.

“The sort you’d notice.”

There was a white line on the floor that people were meant to stand behind while I searched. The woman stood exactly on it, her boots neatly covering the words PLEASE WAIT HERE. She looked about thirty. She had come without a bag, which I took as evidence that she really did expect to leave with a door.

“What bus?”

“The nine. Last Tuesday. Around two.”

“Did you leave it on the bus yourself?”

“Yes.”

“By accident?”

She considered this. “Eventually.”

Behind me were three hundred umbrellas, a dentist’s model of the lower jaw, and a slow cooker containing a serving spoon and no other evidence of a meal. By five the following afternoon, whatever remained would be divided between a charity van and a skip. On Monday the city would outsource lost property to a company whose collection point was in an industrial estate across the river. The company’s website was already up. Its illustration showed a woman being reunited with a purple suitcase, both of them apparently delighted.

I had worked in the office for nineteen years. In that time I had learned that a person who has genuinely lost something is rarely good at describing it. Ask what color their wallet is and they will tell you where they bought it. Ask how many keys were on the ring and they will tell you what the keys open, starting with a house they no longer live in. People attempting to claim someone else’s phone, on the other hand, tend to know the make, model, and retail price.

The woman’s name was Lina. She described the door as blue on one side and white on the other, with a brass handle that pinched if you turned it too far. Then she said, “There’s a little hole near the bottom where my brother tried to put a bolt on his side. He was seven. It didn’t occur to him he’d have to drill all the way through.”

“Was it his bedroom door?”

“It was everybody’s bedroom door at some point.”

I checked the register, though I knew there was no door in it. On Tuesday we’d had a tennis racket, a bag of onions, and half a set of curtains. I remembered the curtains because the driver had submitted two reports, one for each panel, and our software wouldn’t let me persuade him they were traveling together.

“I can ask the depot,” I said. “Leave me a number.”

Lina wrote it on the back of a business card. The front said she was a piano tuner.

“Do most people tell you it’s just been tuned?” I asked.

“No. Most people tell me nobody plays it, as if that ought to have helped.”

She left. I put the card beside the phone, then moved it under the stapler so it wouldn’t get swept into the recycling. I had spent the morning deciding which office supplies were mine. I could account for the mug and the cardigan. The stapler defeated me. I remembered buying it, but I also remembered filling in a form to be reimbursed, and I couldn’t remember whether I’d ever handed in the form. There was no one left in our department to ask.

At the depot a dispatcher called Ben answered. I knew Ben by voice alone. For years he’d told me to hang on a second and then left me to listen to whatever he was eating.

“A door,” he said. “Like off a bus?”

“Off a house.”

“Why would it be on a bus?”

“I was hoping you’d tell me.”

He put me on hold. Through the little speaker came a recording that urged me to consider a career in municipal transport. It listed a pension, discounted travel, and the opportunity to make a difference to someone’s day. The recording had been suggesting this to municipal transport employees for as long as I could remember. Then Ben came back and said yes, there had been a door.

“It’s in the drivers’ room. You want it?”

“Someone does.”

“Ah,” he said. He sounded disappointed.

“Is that a problem?”

“No. We’ve just had our lunch on it.”

By the time I arrived at the depot the next morning, the door had been cleared except for a bottle of hot sauce and a deck of cards. It lay across two filing cabinets in a room with a sink, a kettle, and a notice about the correct procedure for reporting a broken chair. Under the notice was a broken chair.

The driver who’d found the door was called Jo. She was sitting at its far end doing a crossword. I recognized her handwriting before she introduced herself. On lost-property slips, Jo had a way of describing things in terms that made you hope they would be claimed. A WOOL HAT, MUCH MENDED. A CAKE TIN WITH A CAKE STILL IN IT. Once, memorably, A PHOTO OF TWO MEN WITH A FISH THEY ARE CLEARLY VERY PROUD OF.

“She got off to help a man with a pushchair,” Jo said. “Back wheel caught between the bus and the curb. The man got his wheel free and she walked off with him, talking. I waited a bit. In the end someone rang the bell.”

“You could have called after her.”

“I did. I called, ‘Your door!’ She looked right at me and waved.”

Jo set down her pencil. We both looked at the door. On the side facing up, someone had painted over the handle, and years of hands had worn the paint away in a ragged oval. Near the bottom there was a little hole.

“I thought she was giving it to us,” Jo said. “Which was a peculiar thing to do. But it had been a peculiar thing to bring in the first place, so I gave her the benefit of the doubt.”

I called Lina. She said she could come at half past three, between an upright and a baby grand. I asked if she would need help getting the door home. There was a pause long enough for me to hear her turn a page.

“I’m not taking it home,” she said. “My brother’s coming.”

I went back to the office for the final afternoon. Word of the closure had traveled in unpredictable ways. A man came in looking for a pair of binoculars he’d lost in 2006. A woman who’d received three reminders that we had her gym bag turned up to tell me, in person, that we could keep it. Two boys inventoried our stock of footballs with the concentration of surveyors. They found theirs when one of them remembered there was a dog bite in it. His brother said no, that was a hole from the fence. They took the ball, still arguing, both with a hand on it.

Just before three, a woman telephoned about a stuffed rabbit. I asked what it looked like.

“It looks as if it’s been in the washing machine too many times,” she said.

We had four rabbits that met this description. I carried the phone to the shelf and read off their distinguishing features: one ear, green dress, red ribbon, no face.

“Oh God,” the woman said. “No face.”

She was at work until six. I told her I would leave the rabbit at the newsagent’s next door. The newsagent, who had spent nineteen years sending people over to me when they tried to hand lost things to him, said he would make an exception. Then he asked whether we had an umbrella he could borrow.

I gave him a good one.

At half past three I put up the sign that said BACK IN TEN MINUTES. There was no sign for what I meant. I had filed everything that needed filing and emptied the drawer where I kept teabags. I took my cardigan and left the stapler beside the phone.

Lina was already at the depot. She and Jo had turned the door over, blue side up. There were pencil lines near the hinge, each with a date and an initial. Some had been crossed out and redrawn. At the top of the highest line, someone had written IN SOCKS.

“My dad,” Lina said when she saw me looking. “He objected on the grounds that my brother had better socks.”

She put one finger against the lowest mark. It stood a little higher than her knee.

“The builders let me take it,” she said. “They’d put it out with the wood. I went past on my way to a job and there it was. I had to go knocking on the next house to borrow a screwdriver to get the hinges off. Then I missed two buses because the drivers wouldn’t let me on with it.”

“Technically,” Jo said, “neither did I.”

“No, you opened the middle doors and looked the other way.”

“I needed to look that way for unrelated reasons.”

Lina smiled, then checked the time. Her brother was late.

I had assumed the markings were why she wanted the door. So when she asked Jo for a cloth to wipe them off, I said, rather sharply, “Why would you do that?”

Jo found a cloth but didn’t wet it. She set it down by Lina’s hand.

“I thought I’d take a picture first,” Lina said. “Then he could paint it.”

“Your brother?”

“He’s got two bits of kitchen counter balanced on a clothes horse. He says he likes to eat standing up, but he’s been saying that since February.”

I tried to imagine the door in her brother’s kitchen. What I pictured instead was my own father at our kitchen table, working his thumbnail under a drop of dried candle wax. He had done this whenever the wax was there and sometimes when it wasn’t. I couldn’t remember the color of the table. I could remember the noise his thumbnail made against it.

Lina’s brother arrived at four, carrying a tape measure. His name was Sami. He had the same habit Lina did of looking down when he needed to consider a question. When he saw the door he said, “Oh, that one,” with the vague irritation you might reserve for an appliance someone had called you over to fix.

“You don’t have to take it,” Lina said.

Sami pulled out the tape. “I didn’t say I wasn’t taking it.”

He measured the door in both directions, wrote the figures on his hand, and then measured it again. Lina took out her phone and photographed the pencil marks. She did it in sections, shading each patch with her free hand because the light from the window caught the paint. Sami waited until she was done. Then he put his heel against the bottom of the door and stretched the tape up to the line marked IN SOCKS.

“He was right,” he said. “I had hiking socks. Remember those green ones?”

“You wore them to bed.”

“They were comfortable.”

“You wore them in the bath once.”

“That was a different pair of socks.”

For a little while the disagreement required all their attention. I sat in Jo’s chair. Her crossword had one entry left. The clue was *Keep for later*, seven letters. I counted out *reserve* and *set aside*, the latter one letter too long. Jo looked over my shoulder and said, “It’s ‘put by.’ I’ve got two letters wrong somewhere.”

They had come in Sami’s car, a small hatchback with a rear seat that would fold only if you reached through the boot and tugged a loop of webbing. We carried the door out together. It was heavier than it looked and the handle swung open against my wrist. I turned it too far and it pinched.

“Told you,” Lina said. She was at the other end. She couldn’t possibly have seen.

The door went into the car corner first. The boot wouldn’t close over it. Sami inspected the gap. He took the door out again and shifted the passenger seat forward until the headrest nearly touched the windscreen. This time the boot came down. Lina went to open the passenger door and saw what he’d done.

“I’ll take the bus,” she said.

Sami stood with his keys in his hand. “You could come and show me where you think it should go.”

“Have you got anything to put it on?”

“The clothes horse.”

Lina looked through the rear window at the door. “It’ll flatten the clothes horse.”

“Probably,” Sami said. “You could come and watch it happen.”

She got in. There wasn’t room for her knees, so she sat sideways, and Sami reached around her to work the seat belt. As they pulled away, I saw her stretch a hand behind her head to stop the brass handle rattling against the window.

It was twenty to five. I could have gone straight home, but I walked back to the office. The newsagent tapped on his glass as I passed and held up the rabbit by one ear, then set it upright next to the till. He had put it in a paper bag and folded down the sides so that its featureless head stuck out.

Inside the office, I took down the sign. A young man was waiting behind it. He’d lost a black glove on his way to work that morning. We had a whole drawer of black gloves, but none could have come from that morning: the last depot delivery had been the day before. I told him so. Then, because in ten minutes there would be no practical reason not to, I opened the drawer.

He tried on three before he found a right-hand glove that fit. The cuff was a different length from the one he’d brought with him. He pulled down his sleeve and the difference disappeared.

“How much?” he asked.

I shook my head.

He put his hands in his pockets, took them out again, and thanked me. From the window I watched him stop at the corner and take off both gloves to answer his phone.

At five the building manager came for the keys. She offered to wait while I looked around, but I’d already looked around. I handed them over and went outside. A number nine was pulling up across the street. I had never taken it home; it went a longer way, past the swimming baths and over the railway, before joining my usual route. I caught it anyway.

The bus was nearly empty. In the middle, opposite the doors, there was a broad space with two folding seats. I sat in one and tried to work out how Lina had stood with the door. Flat against the window, perhaps, one boot braced behind it for the turns. Or on its long edge across both seats, with the handle jutting into the aisle. Neither seemed right. I thought I might ask Jo, and then remembered Jo hadn’t been looking.

At the swimming baths, an old man got on with a bunch of flowers wrapped in newspaper. He sat across from me and set the flowers on his lap. At the next stop he moved them to the seat beside him to get at his phone. He made a call. Nobody answered. When we reached the railway he stood up, put his phone in his pocket, and stepped toward the doors.

“Your flowers,” I said.

He came back for them. He looked a little annoyed with himself and a little annoyed with me for having witnessed it. Then, as the doors opened, he tucked the newspaper more securely around the stems and said, “She’d never have believed me.”

I didn’t ask who. There wasn’t time, and I liked the way he said it, with such certainty about a conversation he was now not going to have. He stepped down to the pavement. I moved to the window seat and rode the rest of the way home.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: LONG

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A quietly comic, elegiac short story built around a municipal lost-property office and the people who pass through it.

## Grounded reading
The voice is observant and restrained, finding feeling in practical details rather than announcing it. A door’s worn handle and pencilled height marks, a featureless stuffed rabbit, and a borrowed glove become small records of family life, care, and separation. The narrator’s own memories surface obliquely, especially in the remembered sound of their father’s thumbnail on a table. The story invites the reader to notice how people care for one another through modest acts—saving a card from the recycling, leaving a rabbit with a newsagent, opening a drawer after the office has closed—and to accept that not every loss needs to be explained or resolved.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds the ordinary infrastructure of loss: registers, depot calls, drawers of gloves, closing signs, and the gradual outsourcing of a civic service. Against that bureaucratic backdrop, it selects objects marked by use and affection, and gives particular weight to attention: remembering a detail, making room, or noticing when someone is about to leave something behind. Its mood balances dry humor with tenderness, while its ending leaves the narrator riding on rather than offering a grand resolution.

## Evidence line
> I thought I might ask Jo, and then remembered Jo hadn’t been looking.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the carefully recurring lost objects, understated humor, and repeated gestures of practical care make this a distinctive, coherent expression of the story’s values.
